source_paper_text:
Answering Related Questions
Édouard Bonnet
34th Annual European Symposium on Algorithms (ESA 2026)

Sidestep. Given a problem Π, a metric dist over its inputs, and a non-decreasing function
d : ℕ → ℝ_+ ∪ {∞}, we introduce the following problem.

Sidestep(Π, dist, d)
Input: An input I of Π.
Output: A pair (J, Π(J)) with dist(I, J) ≤ d(|I|).

In the above, |I| denotes the size of input I, defined as a natural number. When the main
part of I is a graph, |I| denotes its number of vertices. We further impose that the images of
dist and d can be computed in polynomial time in the size of their arguments. Note that
Π can be a decision or a function problem. And in both cases Sidestep(Π, dist, d) is itself
a function problem. Thus Π(J) lies in {true, false} if Π is a decision problem, and it is the
correct solution to Π on input J, or a special symbol nil indicating the absence of a solution,
when Π is a function problem.

Considered metrics. We will exclusively deal with problems Π whose input is an unweighted
undirected graph, and optionally an integer threshold, and consider two distances between
graphs. Both require that two graphs have the same vertex set for the distance between them
to be finite. For every two graphs G, H, dist_e(G, H) := ∞ if V(G) ≠ V(H) and

dist_e(G, H) := |E(G) △ E(H)|,

otherwise, where △ denotes the symmetric difference. For two graphs G, H on the same vertex
set, V(G), we denote by G △ H the graph with vertex set V(G) and edge set E(G) △ E(H).
We set dist_Δ(G, H) := ∞ if V(G) ≠ V(H) and

dist_Δ(G, H) := Δ(G △ H),

otherwise, where Δ(·) denotes the maximum degree of its graph argument. If the whole
input consists of a graph together with some additional integral, rational, or real parameters
(typically serving as thresholds for a graph property), a finite distance between (G, k) and
(H, ℓ) implies that k = ℓ. Specifically, for every considered distance dist,
dist((G, k), (H, ℓ)) = dist(G, H) if k = ℓ, and dist((G, k), (H, ℓ)) = ∞ otherwise.

A Hamiltonian cycle (resp. Hamiltonian path) is a cycle (resp. path) passing through each
vertex exactly once. A graph is said Hamiltonian if it admits a Hamiltonian cycle.

We treat Hamiltonian Cycle (and similarly Hamiltonian Path) as a function problem. In
particular, an algorithm for Sidestep(Hamiltonian Cycle, dist, d) returns, on input G,
a pair (G′, C) where C is a Hamiltonian cycle of G′, or (G′, nil) if G′ is not Hamiltonian.

We now move to the Dominating Set problem, where given a graph G and an integer
k ∈ [0, |V(G)|], one is asked for a dominating set of size k, or to output nil if none exists.

Question 1. What is the hardness radius of Hamiltonian Cycle under dist_e?
Toward answering Question 1, is it true that for any positive k, Sidestep(Hamiltonian
Cycle, dist_e, n/k) is in FP? We ask the same question for Dominating Set.

Question 2. For any positive k, is Sidestep(Dominating Set, dist_e, n/k) in FP?
In Theorem 11, we show Question 2 for k = e.

The NP-hard Triangle Partition problem inputs an n-vertex graph G with n divisible by 3,
and asks for a partition of V(G) into n/3 triangles. It is straightforward that
Sidestep(Triangle Partition, dist_Δ, 2) is in FP.

Question 5. Is Sidestep(Triangle Partition, dist_Δ, 1) in FP?
target: Prove or disprove: for every fixed real constant c>0, Sidestep(Dominating Set, dist_e, n/c) is in FP. Explicitly, for each fixed c, a polynomial-time algorithm must take every labeled n-vertex graph G and integer threshold q in [0,n], keep q unchanged, produce a graph H on the same vertex set with |E(G) symmetric-difference E(H)| <= n/c, and output either a dominating set of H of size q or nil, with nil correct exactly when no such set exists.
title: Dominating Set Sidestep for every inverse-constant linear edge-edit radius
